title: Once popular for attacking AI, ASCII smuggling is embraced by spammers
gist: Spammers have repurposed ASCII smuggling—an invisible-Unicode technique originally used to sneak hidden instructions past AI models—to hide trigger words from spam filters, driving Microsoft's detected signature volume from about 21,000 to over 2.5 million per day within days of its February onset.

insights.claim: ASCII smuggling hides malicious instructions inside a special range of invisible Unicode 'tag' characters that mimic ASCII text, readable by computers but nearly invisible to humans, and was originally popularized about two years ago to make AI prompt-injection attacks more stealthy.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Establishes the underlying mechanism now being repurposed for a much broader class of attack beyond its original AI-focused use case.
insights.locator: The technique is broadly known as ASCII smuggling

insights.claim: The Unicode tag block contains 128 characters mirroring standard ASCII—for example, U+E0041 mirrors 'A' and U+E0061 mirrors 'a'—letting hidden text be embedded in emails or content without a human reader ever seeing it.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Explains precisely why this technique evades human review while still being machine-readable, the property attackers exploit.
insights.locator: The block of 128 tags mimics a portion of the American Standard Code

insights.claim: Spammers have repurposed ASCII smuggling—originally an AI attack technique—to hide keywords in mass emails and evade spam filters, inverting its original purpose from attacking AI models to attacking spam detectors.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Shows a security technique migrating from a niche AI-safety concern to a mainstream email-abuse vector, widening its real-world impact.
insights.quote: the same property that makes them useful for smuggling instructions into a model also makes them useful for obfuscating keywords before a detector evaluates them,
insights.locator: No longer just for obscuring prompt injections

insights.claim: Microsoft reported that ASCII smuggling signature detections in Microsoft Defender for Office spiked from roughly 21,000 per day to more than 1.3 million beginning in early February, reaching 2.5 million within four days, before falling off sharply in mid-May.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale and speed of adoption of this evasion technique by spammers, useful for gauging the current threat landscape in email security.
insights.locator: Beginning on one day in early February

insights.claim: Spammers embed invisible Unicode characters in the middle of trigger words like 'funding' so literal-text filters searching for terms like 'credit' or 'term' see broken fragments such as 'fun' and 'ding,' while the human recipient still sees the intact word.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, reproducible example of how the evasion defeats naive keyword-based spam filters still in wide use.
insights.locator: Spammers are embedding Unicode in an attempt to evade filters

themes.theme: Why it defeats machine-learning spam filters specifically

insights.claim: Microsoft said the bigger prize for attackers is defeating machine-learning and NLP-based spam classifiers, since inserting an invisible character into a word can cause a tokenizer to split it into unfamiliar sub-word pieces the model no longer recognizes as the original lure term.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Explains why modern ML-based spam detection, not just legacy keyword filters, is vulnerable to this technique, raising the stakes for email security vendors.
insights.quote: The bigger prize for the attacker, though, is not preventing the literal string matches; it is the ML- and NLP-based models that increasingly drive modern spam and phishing classification.

insights.claim: Unless a filtering system takes a picture of a message and runs OCR over the visual image, it may entirely miss this class of attack, since standard email classifiers typically tokenize text rather than reasoning over whole words as a human sees them.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific architectural blind spot in current spam-detection pipelines that security vendors need to address.
insights.quote: Unless a filtering system takes a picture of a message and does OCR extraction over the visual image, it may miss this type of attack.

insights.claim: Spammers have used older techniques like zero-width spaces and non-breaking spaces for decades to evade string-matching filters, suggesting the shift to Unicode tag characters partly reflects that some spam filters had not yet been programmed to detect the newer technique.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Contextualizes this as an escalation in a long-running cat-and-mouse game between spammers and filter vendors rather than an entirely novel threat category.
insights.locator: Using special text to camouflage certain trigger words isn't new

insights.claim: Microsoft published guidance for developers on how to better program spam filters to detect and account for ASCII smuggling.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Signals that a defensive fix is already being distributed to the security community, relevant for tracking how quickly the exploit window closes.
insights.locator: Thursday's post provided guidance on ways developers can program filters
